claims.text: UT Arlington is coordinating a $3.1 million USDA funded project to stop the spread of New World screwworm, a parasite threatening livestock across Texas and other states.
claims.quote: The University of Texas at Arlington is coordinating a $3.1 million project funded by the U.S. Department of Agriculture to stop the spread of New World screwworm, a flesh-eating parasite threatening livestock across Texas and other states.
claims.document: University of Texas at Arlington News Center, UTA leads fight against screwworm, November 12th, 2026

claims.text: Screwworm was declared eliminated from the United States in 1966 and has reemerged. More than 120 confirmed animal cases were reported as of November 12th, most of them in Texas, per the USDA case dashboard.
claims.quote: New World screwworm was declared eliminated from the United States in 1966 but has recently reemerged, with more than 120 confirmed animal cases reported as of Nov. 12, most of them in Texas, according to the USDA's case dashboard.
claims.document: University of Texas at Arlington News Center, UTA leads fight against screwworm, November 12th, 2026

claims.text: Female screwworm flies lay eggs in open wounds, and untreated infestations can be fatal.
claims.quote: Female screwworm flies lay eggs in open wounds or mucous membranes of warm-blooded animals; left untreated, the resulting infestations can be fatal.
claims.document: University of Texas at Arlington News Center, UTA leads fight against screwworm, November 12th, 2026

claims.text: The center of the project is an AI powered smart trap meant to tell wild screwworm flies from sterile ones and females from males.
claims.quote: At the center of the project is an AI-powered "smart trap" capable of distinguishing wild screwworm flies from sterile ones and females from males.
claims.document: University of Texas at Arlington News Center, UTA leads fight against screwworm, November 12th, 2026

claims.text: The trap is meant to capture wild females selectively, because they produce the larvae.
claims.quote: Because wild female flies are responsible for producing the destructive larvae, the trap selectively captures them, allowing for earlier detection of potential outbreaks.
claims.document: University of Texas at Arlington News Center, UTA leads fight against screwworm, November 12th, 2026

claims.text: Shouyi Wang, a UTA associate professor, expects a smart trap prototype by next spring.
claims.quote: The technology builds on previous AI-based fruit fly trap research by Shouyi Wang, a UTA associate professor, who expects to have a smart-trap prototype ready by next spring.
claims.document: University of Texas at Arlington News Center, UTA leads fight against screwworm, November 12th, 2026

claims.text: Current traps capture insects indiscriminately and need extensive manual sorting.
claims.quote: Current screwworm traps capture insects indiscriminately, requiring extensive manual sorting and delaying confirmation of the screwworm’s presence.
claims.document: University of Texas at Arlington News Center, UTA leads fight against screwworm, November 12th, 2026

claims.text: Conventional traps can interfere with the federal sterile fly program because they can't tell sterile flies from wild ones.
claims.quote: They can also interfere with a federal program that releases sterile flies to suppress wild screwworm populations because conventional traps cannot distinguish sterile flies from wild ones.
claims.document: University of Texas at Arlington News Center, UTA leads fight against screwworm, November 12th, 2026

claims.text: Wang says the trap is designed to keep wild flies, especially females, and release sterile flies and other insects.
claims.quote: The smart trap is designed to recognize and selectively retain targeted wild screwworm flies, especially high-risk females, while releasing sterile flies and non-target insects back into the environment.
claims.document: University of Texas at Arlington News Center, UTA leads fight against screwworm, November 12th, 2026

claims.text: Wang says each detection can feed alerts, tracking and risk maps to USDA's Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service.
claims.quote: Connected through a smart-trap network, each detection can feed real-time alerts, location-based tracking and predictive risk maps that provide the USDA’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) with timely, actionable information for faster, more targeted responses.
claims.document: University of Texas at Arlington News Center, UTA leads fight against screwworm, November 12th, 2026

claims.text: The UTA project was one of 40 selected nationwide in roughly $105 million of USDA funding.
claims.quote: UTA's project was one of 40 selected nationwide as part of roughly $105 million in USDA funding.
claims.document: University of Texas at Arlington News Center, UTA leads fight against screwworm, November 12th, 2026

claims.text: The project runs through June 2028, with fieldwork across several states including Texas and in affected regions of Mexico.
claims.quote: The project runs through June 2028, with fieldwork taking place across multiple states, including Texas, and in affected regions of Mexico.
claims.document: University of Texas at Arlington News Center, UTA leads fight against screwworm, November 12th, 2026

claims.text: UTA's Smart Agriculture Research Center leads the project, and its associate director says it aims to build real time surveillance and AI diagnostic tools.
claims.quote: “Our project aims to develop a real-time surveillance system and AI-enabled on-site diagnostic tools to support producers, veterinary practitioners and government agencies,” said Prasanna Gowda, research professor and associate director of UTA’s Smart Agriculture Research Center (SARC), which leads the project.
claims.document: University of Texas at Arlington News Center, UTA leads fight against screwworm, November 12th, 2026

claims.text: Producers and veterinarians would report cases with smartphone images, Gowda says.
claims.quote: Our proposed AI-enabled diagnostic tools will not only allow producers and veterinary practitioners to identify infections faster but also enable them to report directly to our real-time surveillance system with high-resolution images captured on their smartphones.
claims.document: University of Texas at Arlington News Center, UTA leads fight against screwworm, November 12th, 2026

claims.text: By the end of the project UTA aims to deliver a field tested system to APHIS.
claims.quote: By the end of the project, UTA aims to deliver a complete field-tested system to APHIS for ongoing use in nationwide screwworm surveillance and response.
claims.document: University of Texas at Arlington News Center, UTA leads fight against screwworm, November 12th, 2026

claims.text: USDA's research service says its predictive models for New World screwworm use advanced analytic tools and artificial intelligence.
claims.quote: Predictive models use advanced analytic tools and artificial intelligence (AI) to interpret ecological, environmental, and historical information
claims.document: USDA Agricultural Research Service, Tracking the Path of New World Screwworm, 2026

claims.text: USDA says it uses the models to choose where, when and how many sterile flies to release.
claims.quote: USDA uses insights from the models to identify optimal locations, timing, and the number of sterile flies to release
claims.document: USDA Agricultural Research Service, Tracking the Path of New World Screwworm, 2026

claims.text: USDA's research service says the models are already used to pick areas for more livestock and wildlife surveillance.
claims.quote: are already being utilized to select areas for increased livestock and wildlife surveillance
claims.document: USDA Agricultural Research Service, Tracking the Path of New World Screwworm, 2026

claims.text: The modeling work comes from USDA's Knipling-Bushland Livestock Insects Research Laboratory in Kerrville, directed by Kim Lohmeyer.
claims.quote: Kim Lohmeyer, Director of the ARS Knipling-Bushland Livestock Insects Research Laboratory in Kerrville, TX
claims.document: USDA Agricultural Research Service, Tracking the Path of New World Screwworm, 2026

claims.text: USDA's research service says the models can't predict every scenario.
claims.quote: these models cannot predict every scenario, especially those impacted by unpredictable variables
claims.document: USDA Agricultural Research Service, Tracking the Path of New World Screwworm, 2026

claims.text: USDA has built a sterile fly dispersal facility at Moore Air Force Base in Edinburg.
claims.quote: USDA has completed construction of a domestic sterile fly dispersal facility at Moore Air Force Base in Edinburg, Texas
claims.document: USDA APHIS, New World Screwworm Response, 2026

claims.text: An APHIS page says the $8.5 million facility deploys more than 80 million sterile flies per week over Texas and Mexico.
claims.quote: This $8.5 million facility is now used to deploy more than 80 million sterile flies per week over Texas and Mexico.
claims.document: USDA APHIS, New World Screwworm Response, 2026

claims.text: USDA developed a screwworm strain that yields only males for the sterile fly releases.
claims.quote: USDA developed a new strain of New World screwworm that yields only male screwworms for use in the sterile insect dispersal
claims.document: USDA APHIS, New World Screwworm Response, 2026

claims.text: Since July 2025 USDA has monitored more than 100 screwworm specific traps.
claims.quote: Since July 2025, USDA has been actively monitoring more than 100 NWS-specific traps
claims.document: USDA APHIS, New World Screwworm Response, 2026
